title: The Acr-Aca Fusion Protein AcrIF16 Dually Inhibits the Type I-F CRISPR-Cas System Through DNA Sequestration.
authors: Yang, Lingguang; Liu, Xi; Hou, Jiaxin; Liu, Hui; Yin, Peipei; Wang, Hao; Zhang, Yi
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins are natural inhibitors of CRISPR-Cas systems, offering valuable tools for regulating genome editing. Most characterized Acrs function through direct protein-protein interactions with Cas effectors. Here, we report that AcrIF16, an Acr-Aca fusion protein from Pectobacterium parmentieri, inhibits the type I-F CRISPR-Cas system through a DNA-binding-dependent dual mechanism without forming stable complexes with the Csy surveillance complex or the Cas2/3 nuclease. The high-resolution crystal structure of its N-terminal domain (NTD) reveals a canonical helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif that specifically binds inverted repeat sequences upstream of the acrIF16 locus. Structural prediction of the C-terminal domain (CTD) suggests a previously uncharacterized fold, although its functional role remains to be determined. Biochemical assays demonstrate that AcrIF16 binds double-stranded DNA in a sequence-non-specific manner, thereby competing with Csy for target DNA binding and destabilizing pre-assembled Csy-DNA complexes. Furthermore, AcrIF16 inhibits Cas2/3-mediated single-stranded and double-stranded DNA cleavage, an effect attributable to substrate sequestration rather than direct Cas2/3 binding. In vivo, AcrIF16 restores phage plaque formation in E. coli cells expressing the type I-F CRISPR-Cas system, supporting its anti-CRISPR activity. Thus, AcrIF16 employs a DNA-sequestration strategy to block both target recognition and DNA degradation in the type I-F CRISPR-Cas system. This work expands the mechanistic repertoire of anti-CRISPR proteins and highlights DNA-binding Acrs as a distinct class of CRISPR inhibitors.

title: Regulation of the Epstein-Barr Epigenome by Histone Variant MacroH2A.
authors: Castro-Munoz, Leonardo Josue; Yoon, Leena; Karisetty, Bhanu Chandra; Bharti, Aradhana; Tempera, Italo; Soldan, Samantha S; Lieberman, Paul
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Histone variants play an important role in regulating chromatin dynamics of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Here, we investigate the role of histone variant macroH2A in EBV chromatin structure, gene expression and copy number control during latent infection. ChIP-seq analysis in EBV (+) SNU719 gastric carcinoma and Mutu I Burkitt lymphoma cells revealed that macroH2A was most enriched at repetitive DNA elements, including oriLyt, BHLF1, LF3 and terminal repeat (TR) regions of the EBV genome. MacroH2A depletion in EBV-associated gastric cancer cell line SNU719 led to a small increase in some viral lytic genes and increase in viral DNA copy number. RNAseq transcriptomics after macroH2A depletion identified major perturbations in cellular gene pathways, including beta-catenin/TCF signaling and chromatin remodeling. Depletion of macroH2A during EBV lytic reactivation reduced EBV lytic gene activation, but increased EBV DNA copy number. Previous study demonstrated a colocalization and cooperative binding between histone variant H2A.Z and EBNA1. We now show that depletion of macroH2A causes an increase in both H2A.Z and EBNA1 at oriP and cellular binding sites for EBNA1. We also found that gammaH2AX localizes to oriP and that this depends on macroH2A. Finally, we show that CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of macroH2A increases the replication and episome maintenance of oriP-containing plasmids. Taken together, these findings indicate that macroH2A localizes to the repetitive elements of EBV, including oriLyt, and can function to limit H2A.Z and EBNA1 binding at oriP, which alters DNA damage signaling at oriP and limits episomal replication. These findings provide a novel role for macroH2A in maintaining EBV copy number and genome integrity.

title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics.
authors: Qian, Weizhou; Song, Yuxuan; Welch, Joshua D
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distin-guish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

title: Molecular mechanisms of AcrVA-mediated Cas12a inhibition and their potential applications.
authors: Kang, Yong Jun; Park, Hyun Ho
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a is widely used for genome editing because it is simple, efficient, and suitable for multiplex targeting. However, strong or prolonged Cas12a activity can increase unwanted cleavage at off-target sites. This problem is especially important when Cas12a is used in complex microbial communities, where unintended editing may affect non-target microorganisms or mobile genetic elements. Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins are natural inhibitors of CRISPR-Cas systems. Acr proteins targeting type V-A CRISPR-Cas12a systems are called AcrV proteins. Recent structural and biochemical studies have shown that AcrVA proteins inhibit Cas12a through highly different mechanisms. AcrVA1 induces cleavage of Cas12a-bound crRNA. AcrVA2 recognizes the nascent Cas12a polypeptide and promotes translation-dependent degradation of cas12a mRNA. AcrVA3 directly cleaves double-stranded DNA and indirectly reduces Cas12a activity. AcrVA4 allosterically blocks target DNA binding, whereas AcrVA5-AcrVA8 inhibit Cas12a by acetylating important lysine residues. These studies provide a structural basis for using AcrVA proteins as potential Cas12a off-switches. Importantly, AcrV proteins may reduce off-target effects by limiting the strength and duration of Cas12a activity after sufficient on-target editing has occurred. In this mini review, we summarize the structural mechanisms of AcrVA proteins and critically discuss the evidence and experimental requirements for their potential use in controlled Cas12a-based microbial engineering.

title: SLC38A2-Driven Glutamine Metabolic Reprogramming Promotes Hypoxic Survival in Glioblastoma.
authors: Qi, Yanhua; Xia, Huize; Gao, Zijie; Li, Boyan; Pan, Ziwen; Feng, Bowen; Wang, Chuanzheng; Ma, Weiyang; Li, Ruochuan; Qiu, Jiawei; Han, Zhe; Chen, Zheyuan; Tang, Weijie; Wang, Qingtong; Wang, Daiyan; Hao, Leyang; Liu, Junzhi; Zhao, Rongrong; Zhao, Hongyu; Li, Gang; Xue, Hao
abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) is highly refractory to standard therapies, including anti-angiogenic agents such as bevacizumab. While bevacizumab prunes tumor vasculature, it exacerbates intratumoral hypoxia, which drives a metabolically resilient phenotype that limits survival benefits. This study aimed to identify the metabolic dependencies underlying GBM adaptation to hypoxia and to evaluate whether targeting these dependencies could enhance the antitumor efficacy of bevacizumab. Methods: We analyzed the spatial distribution of key metabolites in GBM patients and orthotopic xenograft mouse models using magnetic resonance spectroscopy and chemical shift imaging. A dual-vector hypoxia fate-mapping system paired with an in vivo genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) knockout screen was employed to identify metabolic vulnerabilities within the hypoxic niche. Metabolic flux was analyzed utilizing (13)C(5)-labeled glutamine tracers. The molecular mechanisms governing solute carrier family 38 member 2 (SLC38A2) regulation were investigated using chromatin immunoprecipitation, cycloheximide chase assays, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and co-immunoprecipitation. The efficacy of targeting SLC38A2 was evaluated through structure-based virtual screening and in vivo orthotopic xenograft models treated concurrently with zonisamide and bevacizumab. Results: Imaging and tissue metabolite analyses revealed a spatial metabolic mismatch in the hypoxic tumor core, characterized by lactate accumulation alongside glutamine depletion. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screening identified SLC38A2 as an essential metabolic dependency for GBM cell survival under hypoxic stress. Under hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1alpha) promoted SLC38A2 transcription, while elevated lactate stabilized the SLC38A2 protein through alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1)-mediated lactylation at Lys472. These changes were accompanied by increased glutamine uptake and glutathione biosynthesis, reduced reactive oxygen species levels, and decreased mitochondrial-fission-mediated apoptosis. Pharmacological screening identified the US Food and Drug Administration-approved, brain-penetrant anticonvulsant zonisamide as an inhibitor of SLC38A2. In orthotopic GBM xenograft models, combined treatment with zonisamide and bevacizumab markedly suppressed tumor growth compared with bevacizumab alone. Conclusions: This study defines a spatially organized lactate-glutamine metabolic axis essential for hypoxic adaptation in GBM. The dual transcriptional and posttranslational up-regulation of SLC38A2 represents a critical survival mechanism. This axis can be pharmacologically dismantled by zonisamide, offering a clinically actionable combinational strategy to overcome anti-angiogenic therapy resistance.

title: Comparison of interventional causal structure learning algorithms for gene regulatory network inference.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Causal structure learning offers a promising approach to studying gene regulation in cells, aiming to provide deeper mechanistic insights than purely association-based methods. Theoretical groundwork indicating that interventions improve identifiability of causal structure motivates the use of causal structure learning methods in scenarios with interventional information. RESULTS: This benchmark investigates the ability of existing causal structure learning algorithms to leverage the information revealed by targeted interventions to infer gene regulatory networks (GRNs). In this study synthetic single-cell perturbation data and experimental data from a clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) screen are leveraged, and a suite of causal structure learning algorithms is evaluated on metrics tailored to synthetic ground truth and real biological data respectively. On synthetic data, accurate recovery of GRNs was achieved under favourable conditions: strong interventions, large sample sizes, and low measurement noise. For experimental data, no reliable ground truth is available, so inferred GRNs were assessed indirectly, using observed perturbation effects and curated regulatory annotations. Here, performance remained unreliable, with technical and biological noise and algorithmic scalability as limiting factors. This highlights a current gap between theoretical potential and practical application of causal structure learning for GRNs. CONCLUSIONS: The benchmark provides insight into algorithm strengths and limitations and offers groundwork for further methodological development. We also provide an accessible software package for applying modern causal structure learning to custom datasets and thereby foster future exploration of its potential.

title: Heat stress impairs pharyngeal tooth mineralization via TRPV1 in zebrafish.
authors: Ren, Yujia; Liu, Jingyun; Wang, Zhen; Fu, Jing; Zheng, Huiwen; Xing, Xianghui
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ambient temperature is a fundamental environmental factor that governs a wide range of biological processes in ectotherms. Heat stress is known to disrupt development, yet its impact on specific physiological processes such as tooth biomineralization, and the underlying molecular thermosensing mechanisms, remain poorly understood. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether elevated temperature impairs pharyngeal mineralization in zebrafish and if so, whether the thermosensitive TRPV1 channel mediates this effect. METHODS: Zebrafish larvae were reared at 28  degrees C, 30  degrees C, 32  degrees C or 34  degrees C for 20 days. Pharyngeal tooth mineralization was assessed by Alizarin Red S staining and scanning electron microscopy. Expression of mineralization-related genes (odam, scpp5, scpp1, scpp9) was quantified by qRT-PCR. Tissue morphology was examined by HE staining. TRPV1 involvement was tested by pharmacological inhibition (AMG517) and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated trpv1 knockdown. RESULTS: Higher temperatures progressively impaired tooth mineralization, with patchy staining, changes in ameloblast-like cell morphology, and rough, pitted enameloid surfaces, despite normal survival and morphology. Gene expression of odam, scpp5, scpp1 and scpp9 was consistently downregulated. Both TRPV1 inhibition and trpv1 knockdown substantially rescued the heat-induced defects, restoring mineralization, surface structure and gene expression without affecting viability. CONCLUSION: Heat stress disrupts pharyngeal tooth biomineralization in zebrafish via TRPV1. TRPV1 is essential for this effect, positioning it as a key molecular link between environmental temperature and tooth formation.

title: Fully modified SpyCas9 guide RNAs enable robust genome editing in cells and in vivo.
authors: Vu, Kim Anh; Zhang, Han; Amrani, Nadia; Devi, Gitali; Gaston, Nicholas; Lee, Jonathan; Maitland, Stacy A; Chen, Zexiang; Echeverria, Dimas; Liu, Pengpeng; Ponnienselvan, Karthikeyan; Hanlon, Matthew B; Lucas, Connor; Luk, Kevin; Sousa, Jacquelyn; Cooper, David; Srnka, Alyxandr; Rembetsy-Brown, Julia M; Ansodaria, Aditya Valji; Hedger, Adam K; Wagh, Atish; Bamidele, Nathan; Mir, Aamir; Yamada, Ken; Alterman, Julia F; Khvorova, Anastasia; Wolfe, Scot A; Sontheimer, Erik J; Watts, Jonathan K
abstract: Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA-Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2'-amino-RNA, 4'-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%-100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.

title: Dissecting the molecular machinery of CRISPR-associated transposons.
authors: Wang, Shukun; Singh, Juhi; Rice, Phoebe A; Chang, Leifu
abstract: CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) are naturally occurring mobile genetic elements that combine programmable RNA-guided DNA recognition with transposase-mediated integration, enabling site-selective insertion of kilobase-scale DNA without nuclease-induced double-strand breaks. Current structural and biochemical knowledge can be viewed in terms of three functional modules: the transposase module, which performs DNA cleavage and strand transfer; the AAA+ ATPase TnsC, which forms a recruitment and regulatory platform; and TnsD or CRISPR effector-TniQ targeting complexes, which position this platform at selected DNA sites. Here, we synthesize recent structural and biochemical advances in target recognition, recruitment, donor-end pairing, and strand transfer. Comparisons with Tn7 and phage Mu highlight conserved transposase and ATPase functions and system-specific differences in how these components are organized and regulated. We discuss the implications of these advances for engineering programmable DNA-insertion systems and highlight unresolved questions in CAST transposition.

title: A cilia-associated epithelial alteration axis nominates ERICH3 as an entry point to PI3K engagement in lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Chen, Qiang; Wang, Yixuan; Zhang, Yang; Ying, Shuo; Feng, Huazhuo; Hou, Kai; Zhang, Li; Zhou, Xuexia; Li, Xuebing; Qin, Jianwen; Huang, Dingzhi
abstract: BACKGROUND: LUAD adopts heterogeneous oncogenic signalling states, and bias toward a PI3K-AKT-mTOR-engaged state is not fully explained by canonical pathway lesions. Because membrane-proximal spatial organization can tune receptor-proximal signalling yet is difficult to quantify in human tumours, we used cilia-associated epithelial programs as a hypothesis-generating entry point to identify convergently perturbed candidates and evaluate their relationship with PI3K engagement. METHODS: We performed intersection-based multi-omic prioritization in TCGA-LUAD, evaluated dependency directionality using DepMap/CCLE expression with CRISPR dependency profiles, and tested the functional relationship between ERICH3 loss and PI3K engagement by siRNA perturbation with PI3K-inhibitor rescue. We anchored tumour context using bulk co-expression, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell analyses with ERICH3 stratified by transcript "detection", complemented by CellChat-based communication inference and structure/variant-informed hypothesis nomination. RESULTS: ERICH3 was prioritized through a cilia-informed screen as a convergently attenuated candidate, showed reduced protein in paired LUAD specimens (16/24, 66.7%; P = 0.014), promoter hypermethylation, and favourable survival association. An external DepMap dependency screen nominated PI3K-AKT-mTOR dependency directionality in ERICH3-low contexts (Hallmark NES = - 1.79; P = 1.04 x 10(-)(4)), which was subsequently evaluated functionally in LUAD cell lines. In LUAD cell lines, ERICH3 knockdown increased PI3K-AKT-mTOR phosphorylation and malignant phenotypes, which were attenuated by PI3K inhibition, supporting a functional relationship between ERICH3 loss and PI3K pathway engagement. Multi-scale transcriptomic analyses showed that ERICH3 transcripts were detected predominantly in a mucous epithelial compartment and non-tumour epithelium; CellChat suggested hypothesis-generating immune-interaction signals associated with ERICH3-detected mucous cells. Structural modelling and tumour-variant mapping nominated discrete membrane-proximal regions for mechanism-discriminating follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support a testable model in which attenuation of ERICH3, identified through a cilia-informed epithelial framework, is associated with a PI3K-engaged malignant state in LUAD. The present study does not establish that ERICH3 directly regulates primary-cilium formation, ciliary protein localization, or ligand-induced ciliary signalling; the precise upstream membrane-proximal and/or cilia-related route remains to be defined.

title: Polysaccharide-centered engineering of biomass-derived nanoparticles for precision medicine: From molecular assembly and structural deconstruction to therapeutic design.
authors: Li, Yumeng; Yang, Huan; Xiang, Wenchao; Yang, Xu; Tao, Lu; Jiang, Zhenyu; Han, Shiqi; Chen, Guoqiang; Jia, Haiyang; Liu, Qi
abstract: Polysaccharide-centered engineering of biomass-derived nanoparticles (BNPs) is emerging as a sustainable and biologically compatible strategy for precision medicine. Polysaccharide-derived nanoparticles offer renewable sources, structural diversity, tunable physicochemical properties, and intrinsic biological functions that enable their rational engineering for targeted delivery and therapeutic modulation. This review focuses on cellulose-, chitosan-, alginate-, and hyaluronic acid-based nanoplatforms and examines how their molecular and supramolecular characteristics govern nanoparticle construction, nano-bio interactions, and therapeutic performance. Selected protein-derived systems are discussed where they form hybrid architectures with polysaccharides or provide mechanistic insights directly relevant to polysaccharide nanoengineering. We integrate bottom-up molecular assembly and top-down structural deconstruction as complementary fabrication paradigms and analyze how BNPs navigate physiological barriers through mechanisms including receptor-mediated transport, tight-junction modulation, and stimulus-responsive structural reconfiguration. We further examine their applications in CRISPR-Cas9 delivery and precision immunotherapy, with particular attention to design principles, translational constraints, and opportunities for scalable manufacturing. By linking molecular structure, assembly behavior, biological transport, and therapeutic function, this review provides a polysaccharide-centered framework for the rational development of adaptive biomass-derived nanoplatforms for precision medicine.

title: Large scale CRISPR genome engineering reveal principles of single nucleotide microhomology in precision editing
authors: Shi X; Li C; Li J; Liu Y; Wu Q
abstract: The CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a revolutionary tool with diverse applications in genome engineering; however, the role of nanoscale hydrogen bonds between single nucleotides in precision editing remains unknown. Here we systematically compared A-rich and G-rich PAM-recognizing Cas9 editors through comprehensive analyses of ~37,000 targeting sites with about half million libraries of ~0.36 billion types of editing outcomes. We showed that the A-rich Cas9 editors exhibit stronger editing outcome predictability in comparison with the conventional Cas9 editor of the G-rich PAM. In addition, the A-rich Cas9 editors induce a higher frequency of staggered cleavages, resulting in predictable editing with donor-independent templated insertions. Moreover, we identified distinct DNA sequence motifs for predictable insertions with the A-rich Cas9 editors. In particular, we revealed single nucleotides at the -4 position as MMEJ microhomologies in precision engineering via two or three hydrogen bonds with A-rich or G-rich PAM, respectively. Furthermore, we found that PolQ plays a key role in enhanced random insertions. Finally, we developed a discrete-space diffusion model CRIfuser of deep learning for predicting editing outcomes with staggered cleavage. Together, these findings establish PAM-dependent cleavage geometry as a tunable determinant of Cas9 editing outcomes and provide a framework for predictive and precision genome engineering.
